title: Compound verbs and impersonal constructions

objectives.can: See the simple verb inside a compound, and read impersonal verbs such as oportet, licet and placet.

explanation.summary: Two things make Latin verbs look harder than they are. Many verbs are built from a prefix and a simple verb, and the prefix often changes the look of the stem; and a group of verbs has no personal subject at all and appears only in the third person singular, with an infinitive or a clause doing the work of subject.

sections.heading: A prefix and a simple verb
body: A compound verb is a simple verb with a preposition or other prefix in front: *ascendit* ('he goes up') is *ad-* + *scando*, *introivit* ('he went in') is *intro-* + *eo*, *exiit* ('he went out') is *ex-* + *eo*. The commonest prefixes are ad-, con-, de-, ex-, in-, ob-, per-, prae-, pro-, re-, sub- and trans-. The prefix usually keeps something of its meaning as a preposition, but often shifts it, so the compound has a sense of its own that a dictionary must give. Think of English 'overlook' or 'understand'.

The compound is conjugated just like the simple verb. If you can conjugate *eo*, you can conjugate *abeo*, *exeo*, *introeo* and *transeo*: *abiit*, *exiit*, *introivit*, *transierunt* are all the perfect of the same verb. Look for the simple verb at the end of the word, and take the prefix off.

sections.heading: Assimilation and vowel weakening
body: Two changes disguise the simple verb. First, the last consonant of a prefix often becomes the same as the first consonant of the stem (assimilation): ad- + *fero* gives *affero*, con- + *lego* gives *colligo*, ad- + *porto* gives *apporto*. The edition sometimes keeps the unassimilated spelling (*adfero*), as the library's analyser shows.

Second, the short vowel of the simple verb is often weakened in a compound: a becomes i or e, and ae becomes i. So *facio* gives *conficio*, *perficio*, *deficio* and *proficio*; *lego* gives *colligo*; *capio* gives *accipio* and *excipio*. In the perfect the stem may change again (*fecit*, *perfecit*), and you have to know both. The weakening is a habit rather than a law, so check a dictionary when a compound is unfamiliar.

sections.heading: Impersonal verbs
body: An impersonal verb has no person as subject. It appears in the third person singular (and in the infinitive), and what would be its subject is an infinitive or a clause. *oportet* means 'it is necessary' or 'it is fitting', and in *oportet vos nasci denuo* the thing that is necessary is the infinitive phrase *vos nasci*, 'that you be born again'. Note that the person affected stands in the accusative (*vos*) with the infinitive; with *licet*, *placet* and *expedit* it stands in the dative (*licet tibi*, 'it is permitted to you').

The commonest are *oportet* ('it is necessary'), *licet* ('it is permitted'), *placet* ('it pleases', hence 'it is decided'), *decet* ('it is fitting'), *expedit* ('it is profitable') and the phrase *necesse est* ('it is necessary'). Several of these also have a personal use, with an ordinary subject: in Acts 6:5 *placuit sermo* means 'the word pleased'. Only the construction in which an infinitive or clause serves as subject is impersonal.

sections.heading: Clauses with ut, and the impersonal passive
body: Instead of an infinitive, some impersonals take a clause with *ut* and the subjunctive: *necesse est ut veniant scandala*, 'it is necessary that scandals come'; *expedit vobis ut ego vadam*, 'it is to your advantage that I go'. The commonest of all is *factum est ut*, 'it came about that', which opens countless narratives. The subjunctive is the subject of a later lesson; for now, treat *ut* with the subjunctive as the way to say 'that' after these phrases.

Latin can also use the passive of an intransitive verb impersonally, in the neuter singular: *dictum est* is 'it was said' or, with a dative, 'it was said to the ancients'. Nothing is the subject; the passive simply reports the action. Do not look for a noun to agree with *dictum*. A good English rendering often changes the verb's voice: 'the ancients were told'.

misunderstandings: An impersonal verb is not missing its subject by accident. The infinitive or the *ut* clause is the subject. 'It' in English translations is a stand-in, not a Latin word.
The person affected by *oportet* is in the accusative, but with *licet* and *placet* it is in the dative. Mixing them up gives the wrong meaning.
A compound verb does not always mean the prefix plus the simple verb. *perficio* is not 'make through' but 'complete'. Always read the whole word's sense in context.
*placuit* is not always impersonal. With a noun as subject (*placuit sermo*) it is an ordinary verb, 'it pleased'; with an infinitive (*placuit eligere*) it is impersonal, 'it was decided to choose'.

deeper.heading: Impersonals in Christian Latin
body: Grammarians such as Allen and Greenough list the impersonals by the case that goes with them. In the Vulgate, which translates Greek closely, the patterns follow the Greek: the Greek verbs for 'it is necessary' and 'it is permitted' are rendered by *oportet* and *licet*. This is one reason why these verbs are so common in the Gospels and Acts.

examples.analysis: *Collegerunt* is the perfect of *colligo*, from con- + *lego*. The n of the prefix has become l before the l of the stem. In the previous verse the same verb is the imperative *colligite*: 'gather'. The simple verb inside is *lego*.

examples.analysis: *abiit* and *introivit* are both compounds of *eo*: ab- + *eo*, 'he went away', and intro- + *eo*, 'he went in'. The perfect is *-iit* or *-ivit*, as in the simple verb, and the prefix says in which direction the going is.

quoted.title: John
quoted.english: But I tell you the truth: it is expedient to you that I go: for if I go not, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.

examples.analysis: *expedit* is impersonal: nothing is its subject but the clause *ut ego vadam*, 'that I go'. *vobis* is the dative of the person who benefits: 'it is profitable for you that I go'.

quoted.english: And the saying was liked by all the multitude. And they chose Stephen, a man full of faith, and of the Holy Ghost, and Philip, and Prochorus, and Nicanor, and Timon, and Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch.

examples.analysis: *placuit* is the perfect of *placeo*. Here it has an ordinary subject, *sermo*, and means 'the word pleased'. Compare the use in Acts 15:22, where the same verb takes an infinitive and a dative of the persons and is impersonal.

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.english: And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom. And the rich man also died: and he was buried in hell.

examples.analysis: *Factum est ut moreretur mendicus*: *factum est* is the perfect passive of *facio* used impersonally, 'it came about', and the clause *ut moreretur mendicus* is what came about: 'that the beggar died'. The subject of *moreretur* is *mendicus*, not *factum*. The subjunctive after *ut* is the next topic.
